meta.ogDescription: Not Stephen Covey. QI labels it anonymous; Anaïs Nin printed the wording in 1961 as 'talmudic words'. Covey's own book says something different.

answer.label: Not Stephen Covey — an anonymous saying
answer.authorDates: Origin unknown · close English matches in print from the early 1800s
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator traces close English matches back to the early 1800s and concludes that the origin is not known, so the saying “should be labeled anonymous” ↗. Covey’s own book carries a different sentence, and the familiar wording is the one Anaïs Nin printed in 1961 — presenting it, in her character’s voice, as “the talmudic words.”

source.excerpt: Lillian was reminded of the talmudic words: “We do not see things as they are, we see them as we are.”
trail: Close matches were circulating in English long before any modern self-help book. Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ logs a published 1801 sermon by the cleric Sydney Smith and, in 1831, a piece in the London newspaper The Atlas titled “Things As They Are”: “We cannot see things as they are, for we are compelled by a necessity of nature to see things as we are.”

In 1961 Anaïs Nin printed the familiar wording in Seduction of the Minotaur — but as something her character recalls, not something Nin claims: “Lillian was reminded of the talmudic words…” ↗. The 1961 edition is catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗.

Covey’s own sentence is a different one. Quote Investigator quotes The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (2004 edition, p. 28) as “We see the world, not as it is, but as we are—or, as we are conditioned to see it” ↗; Wikipedia dates the book’s first publication to 1989 ↗ and does not mention this line at all.
Wikiquote files the wording under “Disputed” on its Anaïs Nin page ↗, citing The Seduction of the Minotaur (1961) and noting how the line then travelled onward as a Talmud quotation.
source.excerptNote: As Quote Investigator transcribes it from the 1961 novel. Note the frame: Nin’s character is recalling a saying, which is why this is best described as a line Nin passed along rather than one she wrote.

source.rightsNote: The origin of this exact sentence is unknown, so no rights status can honestly be asserted for the wording itself. The close 19th-century matches Quote Investigator documents sit in public-domain texts but are different sentences; the familiar wording is documented in Anaïs Nin’s Seduction of the Minotaur (1961), a work still in copyright, where she presents the line as one she is quoting rather than writing.

author.name: Anaïs Nin
author.kicker: The writer who put the wording in print
author.heading: Anaïs Nin didn’t claim it either
author.bio: Anaïs Nin was a French-born American diarist, essayist and novelist, best known for the decades of published journals that made her one of the twentieth century’s most quoted writers. Her 1961 novel Seduction of the Minotaur contains the sentence in the form the internet now repeats — but she gave it to a character as a remembered saying, expressly crediting the Talmud rather than herself. She is the reason this wording spread, not the reason it exists; Quote Investigator finds close English matches in print more than a century before her.

copyAttribution: Anonymous — not Stephen Covey. Quote Investigator finds close English matches in print from the early 1800s and concludes the origin is unknown; the familiar wording appears in Anaïs Nin's 'Seduction of the Minotaur' (1961), where she presents it as 'the talmudic words'. Covey's own sentence in 'The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People' reads: 'We see the world, not as it is, but as we are—or, as we are conditioned to see it.'

misattribution.heading: Four credits, none of them holding up
misattribution.intro: This is a saying that collects famous names. The one you most likely saw it under is Stephen Covey — but the sentence in Covey’s book is not this sentence, and the line was in English circulation more than a century before he wrote.

items.why: Covey did put the idea in front of millions of readers, but not in these words. Quote Investigator quotes The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People as “We see the world, not as it is, but as we are—or, as we are conditioned to see it” ↗, and Wikiquote’s Covey page ↗ does not carry the popular wording either.

Nin’s 1961 novel is where the familiar wording is documented, but she framed it as a saying being recalled, not authored — which is why Wikiquote keeps it in its Disputed section ↗ rather than among her sourced quotations.

Nin called it “the talmudic words,” and a 2005 Newsweek piece pinned it to Rabbi Shemuel ben Nachmani in tractate Berakhot 55b. But Quote Investigator notes that the passage there is concerned with the interpretation of dreams, and states flatly that “the assignment to the Talmud does not have strong support” ↗.

The habit predates the internet: an 1876 novel, Henrik Scharling’s Nicolai’s Marriage, already handed “we see things not as they are, but as we are” to Kant. Quote Investigator says plainly that it “has not yet located a version of this maxim in the writings of Kant” ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is the unsatisfying one: Quote Investigator concludes that the origin is not known and that the expression “should be labeled anonymous” ↗ — it was circulating in English in the 1800s, long before either famous name was attached to it.

context.heading: Why this one keeps changing hands
lead: A line this portable needs no author, which is exactly why it keeps acquiring them. It is short, it flatters the reader, and it explains an argument you had last week — so it gets pinned to whichever authority the person quoting it trusts most: a bestselling management guru, a famously quotable diarist, an ancient rabbinic text, a giant of German philosophy. Each credit sounds plausible. None of them is documented.

What the record actually shows is a maxim drifting through English print for well over a century, re-worded slightly by each writer who reaches for it: a sermon, a London newspaper column, a science magazine, an elocution manual, a novel. Anaïs Nin gave it the clean, memorable shape people quote today, and she did so while attributing it to someone else. Covey gave it reach, in words of his own.
detailsBody: 1801 — Sydney Smith, in a published Oxford sermon: “not as the truth of things is, but as we are ourselves.” 1831 — The Atlas of London, in a piece titled “Things As They Are”: “We cannot see things as they are, for we are compelled by a necessity of nature to see things as we are.”

1876 — Henrik Scharling’s novel Nicolai’s Marriage credits Kant with “we see things not as they are, but as we are.” 1890 — G. T. W. Patrick in The Popular Science Monthly. 1891 — S. S. Curry, The Province of Expression. 1914 — the Jersey Journal. 1931 — H. M. Tomlinson, Out of Soundings.

1961 — Anaïs Nin, Seduction of the Minotaur, with the wording that stuck. 2004 — the edition of Covey’s 7 Habits that Quote Investigator cites, carrying its own different sentence. Every item above is drawn from Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗.
context.pull: Nin was quoting. Covey was paraphrasing. Nobody has found who wrote it.
